As readers may have noticed, I do not have a very good opinion of the New York Times.

(Pardon the understatement)

See

Oh, Joy! New Lies From the Czar’s Little Helper, In The New York Times,

Appropriately.

and numerous links

On November 19th The New York Times ran a typically vacuous editorial (excerpts

below) titled Remember the War on Drugs? (Editorial Copyright 2007 The New York

Times Company)

See

Marijuana Prohibition, Media Criticism, Copyrights and the 8th and 9th

Commandments.

It began,

“It is good to see Mexico and the United States working together to battle the

drug cartels that deliver hundreds of tons of illegal drugs to American consumers

every year, killing more than 2,000 Mexicans annually along the way. Still, the

Bush administration’s proposed $1.4 billion counternarcotics aid package falls far

short of what is needed to confront the problem.”

First, the Times should stop using the word “cartels”. The definition of “cartel” is “an

international syndicate, combine, or trust formed esp. to regulate prices and output in

some field of business.”

They should know better. If these groups really were “cartels” there would be far less

violence. The misuse of the word probably began in the coverage of the Colombian

organizations during the days of Pablo Escobar, but this is just one more example of the

war on meaning in prohibitionist propaganda. (Like “sophisticated hydroponic grow

operation” used to describe any grow with two viable plants, most of which are actually

grown in soil.)

Second, most of the “tons” are actually marijuana, although cocaine, heroine and meth

make up most of the dollar volume.

This is an important point, because if marijuana were legalized and law enforcement

could concentrate on hard drugs and human trafficking, those problems would be much

easier to address. Indeed, any discussion of Mexican contraband that avoids even

mentioning the word “marijuana”, is fatuous.

Marijuana is not a problem, but marijuana smuggling is as much a problem as anyother non-toxic contraband as far a border security is concerned, and it is a drain on

very limited enforcement resources that are needed for other things.

See

Will “Plan Mexico” And Its Surge in the Drug War Put Prohibition On the Public

Agenda? Analysis by Richard Cowan

Then they question whether Washington is “serious” enough. That would be a fair

question from a serious organization, but coming from the Times that is a bit much.

See

Transcript of 1996 Conversation Between the Czar and the Former Managing Editor of

New York Times About Medical Marijuana Initiatives Gives Great Insight Into How

Marijuana Prohibition Really Works.

and links

“If Washington is serious about stopping the northward flow of cocaine, heroin

and other drugs, it must begin an aggressive campaign to stop the southward

flow of money and high-powered weapons that finance and arm the cartels. And

there must be a far more serious effort to curb Americans’ use of illicit drugs…”

(emphasis added)

Of course, the Times never reports on the number of marijuana arrests nationally and

only once about their own city that I could find when Giuliani was mayor.

See

More Arresting Developments. Record Marijuana Arrests Go Unreported. “No

Medicine Is Smoked” – So DEA Busts Edibles Maker.

and

Giuliani’s Police State – Like the Marijuana Prohibition That He Loves – Is A

Counterproductive Fraud. 3 Articles.

There is not a lot of talk these days about the war on drugs, but the traffickers are

more than holding their own. The National Drug Intelligence Center estimates

that Andean cocaine arriving in Mexico for transshipment north jumped from 220

tons in 2000 to 380 tons in 2006. Mexican heroin production for the United States

market went from 9 to 19 tons in the same time. In Mexico, defeat is measured in

bodies: more than 2,000 last year and 1,100 in the first six months of 2007,

including drug dealers, police officers, journalists and bystanders…

According to the National Drug Intelligence Center, between $8 billion and $23

billion in proceeds from the drug trade flowed illegally across the border into

Mexico in 2005. The cartels have used that enormous financial clout to corrupt

Mexican law enforcement on an unparalleled scale.

Corruption takes many forms.

See

How Prohibitionism Corrupts the New York Times: “Educating” the Children with the

Party Line, and Undermining Journalistic Integrity. Analysis by Richard Cowan.

The traffickers’ firepower — likened to what American soldiers face inAfghanistan and Iraq— also eclipses the puny arsenal of Mexico’s police forces.

Mexican officials estimate that 90 percent of the guns they confiscate are

smuggled in from the United States.

See

Remembrance and Ignorance: In Afghan fields the poppies grow...

But here is where it gets fun.

“The good news is that Mexico and the United States finally recognize that they

are on the same side in this battle. It is a vast improvement over Washington’s

perennial finger-wagging. Mexico’s resolve to take on drug trafficking, rather than

dismissing it as an unsolvable problem, is also welcome. But it is only a start.”

The editorial ran on November 19th

, so that afternoon I wrote a “letter to the editor”

and waited on the outside chance that they would print it. (Okay, and I still believe in

Santa Claus.)

To the Editors of the New York Times:

From Richard Cowan, Publisher, MarijuanaNews.com

November 19, 2007

Regarding your editorial “Remember the War on Drugs?” – may I suggest that you ask

yourself the same question.

On May 10, 1925 the Times published a story "MEXICO TO JOIN US IN

FIGHT ON DRUGS"

, with the subheading: "Treaty is expected to cut

down smuggling across border and break up gangs of dealers.

"

Unlike today’s editorial, it did briefly mention what it called “marihuana – Mexican

hashish”. Eighty-two years ago, it was already illegal to grow it in Mexico, but roughly 2

million pounds will be seized along the Mexican border this year.

The 1925 article assured us that “the Mexican people are heartily backing the treaty”,

and now you say “Mexico’s resolve to take on drug trafficking, rather than dismissing it

as an unsolvable problem, is also welcome. But it is only a start.”

If this new effort is “only a start”, what was it in 1925? And what will it be eighty-two

years from now?

The “war on drugs” – by one name or another – has been a counterproductive fraud

from the beginning. Your own archives hold the proof.

Richard Cowan

Cowan@MarijuanaNews.com

I publish MarijuanaNews.com

I was National Director of NORML from 1992 to 1995

In 1972, the Times published an Op-ed, which I was asked to write after NationalReview published a cover article I wrote on “Why Conservatives Should Support the

Legalization of Marijuana.”

(MarijuanaNews note: The Times ignores its own archives, but who can blame them.

Marijuana prohibition causes long-term memory loss. The Times is its own “memory

hole.”)
